PLANNING COMMISSION STAFF REPORT AND RESOLUTION NO. PC 26-10
   _____________

  CITY OF AVALON PLANNING COMMISSION

MEETING DATE:  May 20, 2026  AGENDA ITEM:

PREPARED BY:  Kelly Ribuffo, Contract Planner  APP TYPE(S): ZTA

SUBJECT:  A Public Hearing and consideration of a resolution recommending
  approval to the City Council of zoning text amendments to Chapter 9-5,
  Article 6 (Accessory Dwelling Units) of Title 9 of the Avalon Municipal Code,
  implementing housing program 14 as set forth in the 6 Cycle General Plan
  Housing Element and Adoption of Exemption Findings Under the California
  Environmental Quality Act

SUMMARY: A Public Hearing and consideration of a resolution recommending approval to
the City Council of zoning text amendments to Chapter 9-5, Article 6 (Accessory Dwelling Units)
of Title 9 of the Avalon Municipal Code, implementing housing Program 14 as set forth in the 6th
Cycle General Plan Housing Element. The proposed project is exempt from environmental
review under Public Resources Code § 21080.17.

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S):

  1. Conduct a public hearing.

  2. Find that the adoption of the proposed ordinance is statutorily exempt from review under
  the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) under Public Resources Code §
  21080.17.

  3. Adopt Resolution No. PC 26-10, recommending to the Avalon City Council adoption of a
  Resolution approving zoning text amendments to Chapter 9-5, Article 6 (Accessory
  Dwelling Units) of Title 9 of the Avalon Municipal Code.

AUTHORIZING GUIDELINES: AMC Section 9-1.106 authorizes the Planning Commission to
review and take action on recommendations to the City Council on amendments to Title 9 of the
Avalon Municipal code, pursuant to Title 7 of the Government Code (Planning Law).

BACKGROUND: On September 20, 2022, the City Council adopted the 2021 -2029/6th Cycle
General Plan Housing Element. The Housing Element is a state-mandated section of the
General Plan which identifies the housing needs, opportunities, and constraints in the City of
Avalon. The Housing Plan section of the Housing Element further sets forth the City’s goals,
policies and programs to address Avalon’s identified housing needs, including production of 27
new housing units as allocated by the Southern California Association of Governments (SCAG)
Regional Housing Needs Assessment (RHNA) for the 6th review cycle.

The Housing Plan contains 26 programs adopted to implement the goals and policies of the
Housing Element. Some programs require one-time code amendments, while others have
ongoing review schedules that require monitoring legislative actions and regular updates to the
Avalon Municipal Code (AMC). Over the next several months, the Planning and Building
Department will bring forth a series of code amendments for consideration to implement all of
   Page 2of6

the housing programs to ensure the City continues to be compliant with State law. The
amendments proposed at this time are intended to address the requirements of Program #14
(Accessory Dwelling Units).

DISCUSSION AND RECOMMENDATIONS: Accessory dwelling units (ADU5) and junior
accessory dwelling units (JADUs) help meet the City’s housing needs for all income levels
and also provide a housing resource for seniors and low- and moderate-income households
throughout the entire community. In accordance with State law, accessory units (also known
as second units or granny flats) are allowed by right in all residential zones within the City.
Chapter 9-5, Article 6, Accessory Dwelling Units, provides specific development standards
and processing requirements for ADUs.

Program #14 requires that the City continue to amend the ordinance based on future
changes to State law and work with the California Department of Housing and Community
Development (HCD) to ensure continued compliance with State law. The City will also
continue to monitor the extent of ADU production to ensure that the ordinance modifications
are successful and that the Housing Element goals can be met.

SB 543, AB 1154, and AB 46, adopted in 2025, are the most recent legislative acts that
include multiple updates to State ADU law which clarify the development requirements for
ADUs. Below is a summary of the substantive amendments proposed to comply with current
State law requirements:

  •  Update Government Code and Health and Safety Code legal references throughout.

  •  Remove the “building-permit only” processing option. All ADUs and JADUs now
  require approval of a ministerial ADU permit and building permits. (Section 9-5.604.a)

  •  Identify the Planning Commission as the review authority of appeals of
  determinations made by staff regarding the completeness and/or denial of ADU
  permit applications. (Section 9-5.604.c.1 .f and 9-5.604.c.5)

  •  Clarify that ADU permits are not exempt from compliance with the Coastal
  Development Permit (CDP) review process. If required, CDP applications must be
  approved or denied with 60 days of an ADU permit application being deemed
  complete. (Section 9-5.604.c.6). The ability to appeal a CDP for an ADU to the
  Coastal Commission has also been eliminated by state law.

  •  Establish two classes of ADUs depending on the governing State laws applicable to
  their processing and clarify the number of detached ADUs permitted on a lot with
  proposed multi-family development. (Section 9-5.605)

  o  Class I ADUs and JADUs are approved under Government Code section
  66323. The Class 1 category allows for the creation of ADU5 on lots in a
  residential or mixed use zone and JADUs on lots zoned for single-family
  residences subject to certain applicable standards, as specified by state law.

  •  On a lot with a single-family use, up to one attached ADU, one detached
  ADU, and one JADU may be constructed.
   Page3of6

  •  On a lot with an existing multi-family use (two or more units), one or
  more ADUs may be created within portions of existing multifamily dwelling
  structures that are not used as livable space (such as storage rooms,
  garages, etc.) up to a quantity equal to 25% of the existing multi-family
  dwelling units.

  •  On a lot with a proposed multi-family use (two or more units),up to two
  detached ADUs may be constructed.

  •  On a lot with an existing multi-family use (two or more units), up to eight
  detached ADUs may be constructed, with the quantity not to exceed the
  number of existing primary dwelling units on the lot.

  o  Class 2 ADUs are approved pursuant to Government Code sections 66314
  through 66322. The Class 2 category is subject to other local object development
  standards (e.g. size, FAR, lot coverage, minimum open space, and others).

  •  Update the owner-occupancy requirements for JADUs. (Section 9-5.606.g.2) JADU5
  that do not share sanitation facilities with the primary dwelling unit structure may
  potentially be exempt for the owner-occupancy requirement.

  •  Clarify timing for issuance of a certificate of occupancy (COO) for ADUs and JADUs
  in relationship to the COO for a primary dwelling unit. (Section 9-5.606.k)

  •  Clarify that ADUs and JADUs under 500 square feet of interior living area are not
  subject to school fees under Education Code section 17620. (Section 9-5.608.a.2)

  •  Clarify that a direct utility connection is required for separate conveyance of an ADU
  when separate conveyance is allowed by code. (Section 9-5.608.b.2)

Complete amendment language is included in the draft ordinance attached to the proposed
resolution (Attachment 1) and strike-through amendment text (Attachment 2). It is the opinion
of staff that the proposed amendments comply with existing State law concerning ADUs and
fully implements Program #14 of the 6th Cycle Housing Element.

GENERAL PLAN, LAND USE, AND ZONING COMPLIANCE:

Compliant pursuant to Government Code section 66314(c). The proposed amendments to the
AMC are consistent with the City’s General Plan because they will implement Program #14 of
the City’s 2021-2029 6th Cycle General Plan Housing Element, and the proposed amendments
implement Policy 11-9 of the Land Use Element, which provides for infill of the City Center area
and increasing the intensity of development on vacant and underutilized properties, in lieu of
outward development, where appropriate

ENVIRONMENTAL DETERMINATION: Under California Public Resources Code section
21080.17, CEQA does not apply to the adoption of an ordinance by a city or county implementing
the provisions of Chapter 13 of Division I of Title 7 of the California Government Code, which is
California’s ADU law. Therefore, the proposed ordinance is statutorily exempt from CEQA in that
the proposed ordinance implements state ADU law.

SUBJECT:  Repair and Maintenance of City of Avalon Fire Engine 7

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): 1. Amend the Fiscal Year 2025-26 Budget, adding an additional
$75,000 to account #10245-6781 to support the rehabilitation of the City-owned Fire Engine 7.
2. Ratify prior action and authorize an additional expenditure of an amount not-to-exceed
$75,000 to Performance Truck Repair, a sole source vendor, for the rehabilitation of the City-
owned Fire Engine 7 for a total repair of $96,192.72.

REPORT SUMMARY: On March 3, 2026, City Council authorized repairs and maintenance for
an amount not-to-exceed $30,000 for essential repairs to Fire Engine 7.

Engine 7 was driven from the Avalon Freight Services in San Pedro to Azusa CA. While driving
the vehicle to the maintenance center, multiple alarms and lights came on in the cab. The vehicle
was initially scheduled to have its pump repaired. However, once the pump was removed,
mechanics were unable to get the same exact pump replaced. Mechanics had to modify almost
every component for the new pump to be installed.

As the vehicle was already at the mechanic, City Staff determined there was an economic
advantage to completing all work necessary to make Engine 7 safe to operate and pass required
regulatory testing.

It took them 230 hours of labor to mock-up the new pump assembly from Waterous, the new
pump sits an inch higher due to the new plates. They also had to mark and weld new holes for
the pump on the pump panel and intakes, install the new tank to pump and the pipe in the water
tank that had multiple holes in it, installed a new primer, the old one was missing pieces, installed
new flappers, pipes, gaskets etc. Additional work includes installation of a new auxiliary inlet on
the diver’s side, and a new radiator.

To meet its financial obligations, City Staff recommends the City Council amend the Fiscal Year
2025-26 Budget, adding an additional $75,000 to account #10245-6781 to support the
rehabilitation of the City-owned Fire Engine 7. City Staff also recommends the City Council ratify
prior action and authorize an additional expenditure of an amount not-to-exceed $75,000 to
Performance Truck Repair, for a total repair of $96,192.72.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Vehicle Repairs and Maintenance is outlined En the Fiscal Year 2025-26
Budget fund 10245-6781.
 CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The City budget would
not accurately reflect the repair costs.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Implement City Council direction.

SUBJECT:  Ovivo Screen Lease Extension

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Authorize the City Manager, or his designee, to extend a
lease agreement with Ovivo for a Micro Ozzy Cup Screen for an additional three-month
period, for a not-to-exceed sum of $40,000.

REPORT SUMMARY: On December 18, 2025 a failure occurred on a force main at the
City of Avalon’s Wastewater Treatment Plant (MAJTP). City personnel, working
cooperatively with the City’s WWTP contractor PERCWater (PERC), were able to
stabilize the force main and install a temporary bypass.

However, while City personnel were working to make permanent repairs at the MNTP
headworks the initial stage of the wastewater treatment process where raw sewage
  —

enters the system  — a second failure occurred when a structural beam that supports
critical equipment collapsed resulting in the headworks grit screen falling into the grit tank.
This cascade of unfortunate events led to the decision to take the headworks out of
operation and deploy a leased piece of equipment to perform the process.

Avalon Municipal Code (AMC) Section 4-2.05 designates the City Manager as the
Director of Emergency Services and grants him the authority to request the City Council
proclaim the existence of a “local emergency”.

Due to the significance of the headworks and the scope of necessary repairs, the City
Manager made the finding that an emergency exists and, under his emergency authority,
authorized a lease with Ovivo for an Ovivo Micro Ozzy Cup Screen.

The City anticipated leasing the screen for an approximate 2 to 3-month period for a not-
to-exceed sum of $55,000. The not-to-exceed sum included the rental rate as well as
anticipated mobilization, demobilization, installation and freight fees. During the time the
leased screen is in service, the City and PERC will determine if the screen is an
appropriate long-term replacement, and the City may ultimately purchase the screen from
Ovivo pending City Council approval.
  —

On February 2, 2026, the City Council ratified prior action taken by the City Manager
including approval of the lease agreement.
 While the leased screen has been in place, PERC and other City contractors have worked
to make significant repairs to the WWTP grit chamber. These repairs are scheduled to be
completed in the next 60 days. At that time, the City and PERC will make a determination
if they should keep the Ovivo Micro Ozzy Cup Screen, or return it. If the City team
determines the screen should be kept, their recommendation will come to the City Council
for their consideration and approval.

FISCAL IMPACTS: These contracted services will be allocated to Fiscal Year 2026-27
Capital Improvement Program Major Sewer Projects CIP #205012, Fund #10850-6521.
  —

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Vital infrastructure.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The City
Manager will not have authority to procure equipment for necessary repairs to the WWTP.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: City Staff will work to determine additional scope.

ADVERTISING, NOTICE AND PUBLIC CONTACT: The item was properly listed on the
posted agenda pursuant to the Brown Act.

SUBJECT:  Award of Construction Contract Wastewater Treatment
  —

  Plant Lab Roof Modification and Casino Showers and
  Restrooms Roof Remediation

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Authorize the City Manager or his designee to negotiate
and execute a contract with Best Contracting Services, Inc. for the Wastewater Treatment
Plant Lab Roof Modification of $145,000 and Casino Showers & Restrooms Roof
Remediation of $125,000 for a total project contract amount not-to-exceed $270,000 as
budgeted in the City’s Fiscal Year 2026-2027 Capital Improvement Plan, Project No.
275004 and No. 277001. The following funding accounts will be used 11325-6552
(Saltwater Fund $58,000), 10825-6521 (Sewer Fund $87,000), and 10470-6679 (Harbor
Fund $145,000).

REPORT SUMMARY: The City-owned roofs at the Wastewater Treatment Plant (WWTP)
Laboratory and the Casino Showers and Restroom Building have reached the end of their
useful service lives and have experienced ongoing deterioration due to age and
continuous exposure to the harsh coastal marine environment. The deteriorated roofing
systems have resulted in water intrusion, increasing maintenance costs, and the potential
for damage to City facilities and equipment.

To address these deficiencies, the City prepared plans and specifications and solicited
formal competitive bids in accordance with Avalon Municipal Code Section 3-4.106. The
project includes removal of the existing roofing systems and installation of new roofing
systems, together with related repairs and improvements necessary to provide long-term
protection of both facilities. The project was publicly advertised, and bids were due on
Friday, June 19, 2026. One responsive bid was received from Best Contracting Services,
Inc.

 CONTRACTOR  BASE BID
 Best Contracting Services, Inc.  $21 1 400.00

Staff have reviewed the bid package submitted by Best Contracting Services, Inc. and
determined the bid is responsive and the contractor possesses the qualifications,
licensing, and experience necessary to successfully complete the project. Although only
one bid was received, Staff believe the bid is fair and reasonable given the specialized
nature of roofing work on Catalina Island, prevailing wage requirements, mobilization
 costs associated with transporting labor and materials to the island, and current
construction market conditions. Construction is anticipated to begin following contract
execution and procurement of materials, with completion for both projects expected in
Fall 2026. Time is of the essence to mobilize and complete this project before the winter
storm season begins, since it is predicted to be a Super El Nino. The project timeline for
construction is 60 days from the notice to proceed. Staff recommends awarding the
construction contract to Best Contracting Services, Inc.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Wastewater Treatment Plant Lab Roof Modification of $145,000 and
Casino Showers & Restrooms Roof Remediation of $125,000 for a total project contract

  3.3.4  Procedure for Resolving Claims.

  3.3.4.1  Prerequisites. Contractor shall timely comply with any and all
requirement of the Contract Documents pertaining to notices and requests for changes to the
Contract Time or Contract Price, including but not limited to all requirements of Article 9.1, as a
prerequisite to filing any claim governed by this Article. The failure to timely submit a notice of
delay or notice of change, or to timely request a change to the time for completion or Contractor’s
compensation, or to timely provide any other notice or request required herein shall constitute a
waiver of the right to further pursue the claim under the Contract or at law.

  3.3.4.2  Intent. Effective January 1, 1991, Section 20104 et seq., of the
California Public Contract Code prescribes a process utilizing informal conferences, non-binding
judicial supervised mediation, and judicial arbitration to resolve disputes on construction claims
of $375,000 or less. Effective January 1, 2017, Section 9204 of the Public Contract Code
prescribes a process for negotiation and mediation to resolve disputes on construction claims.
The intent of this Article is to implement Sections 20104 et seq. and Section 9204 of the California
Public Contract Code. This Article shall be construed to be consistent with all applicable law,
including but not limited to these statutes.

  3.3.4.3  Claims. For purposes of this Article, “Claim” means a separate
demand by the Contractor for:

  (A)  An adjustment to the time for completion including, without limitation, for
  relief from damages or penalties for delay assessed by the City;

  (B)  Payment by the City of money or damages arising from Work done by or
  on behalf of the Contractor pursuant to the Contract, payment for which is
  not otherwise expressly provided or to which the Contractor is not
  otherwise entitled; or

  (C)  An amount the payment of which is disputed by the City.

  A “Claim” does not include any demand for payment for which the Contractor has
  failed to provide notice, request a Change Order, or otherwise failed to follow any

Article must be filed no later than thirty (30) Days after a request for change has been denied in
whole or in part or after any other event giving rise to the Claim. The Claim shall be submitted in
writing to the City and shall include on its first page the following words in 16 point capital font:

  3.3.4.8  Mediation. Within 10 business days following the conclusion of
the meet and confer conference, if the Claim or any portion of the Claim remains in dispute, the
City shall provide the Contractor a written statement identifying the portion of the Claim that
remains in dispute and the portion that is undisputed. Any payment due on an undisputed portion
of the Claim shall be processed and made within 60 Days after the City issues its written
statement. Any disputed portion of the Claim, as identified by the Contractor in writing, shall be
submitted to nonbinding mediation, with the City and the Contractor sharing the associated costs
equally. The public entity and Contractor shall mutually agree to a mediator within 10 business
days after the disputed portion of the Claim has been identified in writing, unless the parties agree
to select a mediator at a later time.

  (A)  If the parties cannot agree upon a mediator, each party shall select a
  mediator and those mediators shall select a qualified neutral third party to
  mediate with regard to the disputed portion of the Claim. Each party shall
  bear the fees and costs charged by its respective mediator in connection
  with the selection of the neutral mediator.

  (B)  For purposes of this Article, mediation includes any nonbinding process,
  including, but not limited to, neutral evaluation or a dispute review board,
  in which an independent third party or board assists the parties in dispute
  resolution through negotiation or by issuance of an evaluation. Any
  mediation utilized shall conform to the timeframes in this Article.

  (C)  Unless otherwise agreed to by the City and the Contractor in writing, the
  mediation conducted pursuant to this section shall excuse any further
  obligation under Section 20104.4 to mediate after litigation has been
  commenced.

  (D)  The mediation shall be held no earlier than the date the Contractor
  completes the Work or the date that the Contractor last performs Work,
  whichever is earlier. All unresolved Claims shall be considered jointly in a
  single mediation, unless a new unrelated Claim arises after mediation is
  completed.

  3.3.4.9  Procedures After Mediation. If following the mediation, the
Claim or any portion remains in dispute, the Contractor must file a Government Code claim
pursuant to Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 900) and Chapter 2 (commencing with Section
910) of Part 3 of Division 3.6 of Title I of the Government Code prior to initiating litigation. For

  3.3.4.10 Civil Actions. The following procedures are established for all

  15 Days from the commencement of the mediation unless a time
  requirement is extended upon a good cause showing to the court.

  (B)  If the matter remains in dispute, the case shall be submitted to judicial
  arbitration pursuant to Chapter 2.5 (commencing with Section 1141.10) of
  Title 3 of Part 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, notwithstanding Section
  1114.11 of that code. The Civil Discovery Act of 1986 (Article 3
  (commencing with Section 2016) of Chapter 3 of Title 3 of Part 4 of the
  Code of Civil Procedure) shall apply to any proceeding brought under this
  subdivision consistent with the rules pertaining to judicial arbitration. In
  addition to Chapter 2.5 (commencing with Section 1141.10) of Title 3 of
  Part 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, (A) arbitrators shall, when possible,
  be experienced in construction law, and (B) any party appealing an
  arbitration award who does not obtain a more favorable judgment shall, in
  addition to payment of costs and fees under that chapter, also pay the
  attorney’s fees on appeal of the other party.
